title: Prefixed verbs of motion
objectives: I can say that someone arrives, leaves, goes in, drops in, crosses, reaches, passes, approaches, goes around or moves away, with the prefixed verbs of motion such as 'прийти́', 'ви́йти' and 'перейти́'.

I can form the aspect pair of a prefixed verb of motion: a perfective from the verb of one direction ('прийти́', 'приї́хати') and an imperfective from the general verb ('прихо́дити') or from '-їжджа́ти' ('приїжджа́ти').
I can use the preposition that goes with each prefix: 'ви́йти з', 'зайти́ до', 'перейти́ че́рез', 'дійти́ до', 'відійти́ від', 'пройти́ повз' and 'іти́ уздо́вж'.
I can describe a route through a city, guide someone by phone, invite a friend over and talk about moving to a new home.
I can explain why 'іти́' is written 'йти' in 'прийти́' and 'ійти' in 'відійти́', why 'від’ї́хати' has an apostrophe and 'приї́хати' does not, and why 'ви́йти' is stressed on 'ви-' in every form.

vocabulary.source: to arrive, to come, on foot
vocabulary.note: 'Прийду́', 'при́йдеш', 'при́йдуть'; past 'прийшо́в', 'прийшла́', 'прийшли́'. Imperfective partner 'прихо́дити'. A bus or a train that arrives also 'прихо́дить'.

example.target: Окса́на прийшла́ на робо́ту о дев’я́тій.
example.source: Oksana got to work at nine.
example.source_literal: Oksana arrived to work at ninth.

vocabulary.source: to arrive, to come, on foot
vocabulary.note: 'Прихо́джу', 'прихо́диш', 'прихо́дять'. Perfective partner 'прийти́'. The imperatives 'Прихо́дь!' and 'Прихо́дьте!' invite someone to come over.

example.target: Сем щодня́ прихо́дить в університе́т о во́сьмій.
example.source: Sam gets to the university at eight every day.
example.source_literal: Sam every-day arrives to university at eighth.

vocabulary.source: to go out, to leave, to get off
vocabulary.note: 'Ви́йду', 'ви́йдеш'; past 'ви́йшов', 'ви́йшла'. Stressed on 'ви-' in every form. Imperfective partner 'вихо́дити'. The place left takes 'з' and the genitive.

example.target: Ми ви́йшли з кафе́ о деся́тій.
example.source: We left the café at ten.
example.source_literal: We went-out from café at tenth.

vocabulary.source: to go out, to leave, to get off
vocabulary.note: 'Вихо́джу', 'вихо́диш'. Perfective partner 'ви́йти'. A window that faces something 'вихо́дить' onto it: 'Ві́кна вихо́дять на парк.'

example.target: Ми зазвича́й вихо́димо з до́му о сьо́мій.
example.source: We usually leave home at seven.
example.source_literal: We usually go-out from home at seventh.

vocabulary.source: to drop in, to call at; to go into
vocabulary.note: 'Зайду́', 'за́йдеш'; past 'зайшо́в', 'зайшла́'. Imperfective partner 'захо́дити'. A person takes 'до' and the genitive; a place takes 'у', 'в' or 'на' and the accusative, or 'до' and the genitive.

example.target: Пі́сля робо́ти я зайду́ до Андрі́я в кафе́.
example.source: After work I'll drop in on Andrii at the café.
example.source_literal: After work I will-drop-in to Andrii into café.

vocabulary.source: to drop in, to call at; to go into
vocabulary.note: 'Захо́джу', 'захо́диш'. Perfective partner 'зайти́'. 'Захо́дь!' and 'Захо́дьте!' are what you say to invite a visitor in.

example.source: Come in, please!

vocabulary.source: to cross, on foot
vocabulary.note: 'Перейду́', 'пере́йдеш'; past 'перейшо́в'. Imperfective partner 'перехо́дити'. What is crossed is in the accusative, with or without 'че́рез'.

example.target: Ми перейшли́ ву́лицю й зайшли́ в кафе́.
example.source: We crossed the street and went into the café.
example.source_literal: We crossed street and dropped-in into café.

vocabulary.source: to cross, on foot
vocabulary.note: 'Перехо́джу', 'перехо́диш'. Perfective partner 'перейти́'.

example.source: I cross this square every day.

vocabulary.source: to reach, to get as far as, on foot
vocabulary.note: 'Дійду́', 'ді́йдеш'; past 'дійшо́в'. The goal takes 'до' and the genitive. Imperfective partner 'дохо́дити'. 'Як дійти́ до...?' is how you ask the way on foot.

example.source: Excuse me, how do I get to the railway station?

vocabulary.source: to move away, to step away; to depart, of a train
vocabulary.note: 'Відійду́', 'віді́йдеш'; past 'відійшо́в'. What one moves away from takes 'від' and the genitive. Imperfective partner 'відхо́дити'.

example.source: The train left at seven.

vocabulary.source: to pass, to walk through, to walk past
vocabulary.note: 'Пройду́', 'про́йдеш'; past 'пройшо́в'. Imperfective partner 'прохо́дити'. Past something is 'повз', through something 'че́рез'.

example.source: We walked through the park.

vocabulary.source: to arrive, to come, by vehicle
vocabulary.note: 'Приї́ду', 'приї́деш', 'приї́дуть'; past 'приї́хав', 'приї́хала'. Imperfective partner 'приїжджа́ти'.

example.target: Сем приї́хав до Ки́єва рік тому́.
example.source: Sam came to Kyiv a year ago.
example.source_literal: Sam arrived to Kyiv year ago.

vocabulary.source: to arrive, to come, by vehicle
vocabulary.note: 'Приїжджа́ю', 'приїжджа́єш', 'приїжджа́ють', like 'чита́ти'. Perfective partner 'приї́хати'. 'Приїжджа́й!' invites someone to visit from another place.

example.source: My parents often come to see me.

vocabulary.source: to move house; to cross, by vehicle
vocabulary.note: 'Переї́ду', 'переї́деш'; past 'переї́хав'. Imperfective partner 'переїжджа́ти'. The new home takes 'у', 'в' or 'на' and the accusative, or 'до' and the genitive.

example.target: Мину́лого ро́ку на́ші сусі́ди переї́хали до Льво́ва.
example.source: Last year our neighbors moved to Lviv.
example.source_literal: Of-last of-year our neighbors moved to Lviv.

vocabulary.source: from, away from
vocabulary.note: With the genitive. Away from a thing ('від вікна́') and from a person ('від лі́каря'); out of a place is 'з' ('з до́му').

example.source: I'm coming from the doctor's.

vocabulary.source: past, by
vocabulary.note: With the accusative.

example.target: Щодня́ я прохо́джу повз цей магази́н.
example.source: Every day I walk past this shop.
example.source_literal: Every-day I pass past this shop.

vocabulary.source: along
vocabulary.note: With the genitive. After a vowel it is 'вздовж', by the euphony rules.

example.source: Taras was running along the Dnipro.

vocabulary.source: home, to one's home
vocabulary.note: Answers 'куди́?', as 'вдо́ма' answers 'де?'. Built from 'до' and 'дім'.

example.source: Taras went home at six.

vocabulary.source: exit, way out
vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ви́ходу'. Built from 'ви-' and the stem of 'ходи́ти', like 'вихо́дити'.

example.source: Where is the way out of the metro?

vocabulary.source: entrance, way in
vocabulary.note: Genitive 'вхо́ду'. Built on the stem of 'вхо́дити', to enter.

example.source: The entrance to the museum is on the left.

dialogues.title: From the station by phone
dialogues.context: Sam's friend Marko, a Canadian whose family is Ukrainian, has come to Kyiv by train for the first time. Sam guides him by phone from the railway station to his apartment. The two friends say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: Се́ме, приві́т! Я вже в Ки́єві. По́їзд прийшо́в о дев’я́тій.
lines.source: Sam, hi! I'm in Kyiv now. The train got in at nine.
lines.source_literal: Sam, hi! I already in Kyiv. Train arrived at ninth.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Приві́т, Ма́рку! Ти ще в по́їзді?
lines.source: Hi, Marko! Are you still on the train?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Marko! You still in train?

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: Так, але́ ви́йду за хвили́ну. Куди́ мені́ йти?
lines.source: Yes, but I'll get off in a minute. Where should I go?
lines.source_literal: Yes, but I-will-go-out within minute. Where-to to-me to-go?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ви́йди з по́їзда і йди до вокза́лу. Пройди́ че́рез вокза́л і ви́йди на пло́щу.
lines.source: Get off the train and walk to the station building. Go through the station and come out onto the square.
lines.source_literal: Go-out from train and go to station. Pass through station and go-out onto square.

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: Я на пло́щі. Тут бага́то таксі́. Мо́жна взя́ти таксі́?
lines.source: I'm on the square. There are lots of taxis here. Can I take a taxi?
lines.source_literal: I on square. Here many taxis. Possible to-take taxi?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Не бери́ таксі́, я живу́ бли́зько. Перейди́ пло́щу і йди ліво́руч уздо́вж ву́лиці.
lines.source: Don't take a taxi, I live close by. Cross the square and walk left along the street.
lines.source_literal: Not take taxi, I live near. Cross square and go to-the-left along street.

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: Іду́. Право́руч я ба́чу вели́кий парк.
lines.source: On my way. I can see a big park on the right.
lines.source_literal: I-go. On-the-right I see big park.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так. Пройди́ повз парк і дійди́ до світлофо́ра.
lines.source: Yes. Walk past the park and go as far as the traffic light.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Pass past park and reach to traffic-light.

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: Дійшо́в. Тут перехре́стя й мале́ кафе́.
lines.source: I'm there. There's an intersection here and a small café.
lines.source_literal: Reached. Here intersection and small café.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Це кафе́ мого́ дру́га Андрі́я. Перейди́ ву́лицю, але́ не захо́дь у кафе́. Ми за́йдемо туди́ ра́зом уве́чері.
lines.source: That's my friend Andrii's café. Cross the street, but don't go into the café. We'll drop in there together this evening.
lines.source_literal: This café of-my of-friend of-Andrii. Cross street, but not drop-in into café. We will-drop-in there together in-evening.

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: До́бре. А де ти живе́ш?
lines.source: All right. And where do you live?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: За кафе́. Обійди́ його́ право́руч. Я чека́ю тебе́ бі́ля вхо́ду.
lines.source: Behind the café. Go around it on the right. I'm waiting for you by the entrance.
lines.source_literal: Behind café. Go-around it on-the-right. I wait you near entrance.

lines.speaker: Марко́
lines.target: Ба́чу тебе́, Се́ме!
lines.source: I can see you, Sam!
lines.source_literal: I-see you, Sam!

dialogues.title: Moving day
dialogues.context: Oksana has rented a bigger apartment and is moving on Saturday. Taras meets her at Andrii's café. The two friends say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Окса́но, я чув, що ти переїжджа́єш. Це пра́вда?
lines.source: Oksana, I heard you're moving. Is that true?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, I heard that you move. This truth?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так! У субо́ту я переїжджа́ю зі старо́ї кварти́ри в нову́.
lines.source: Yes! On Saturday I'm moving from my old apartment to a new one.
lines.source_literal: Yes! In Saturday I move from old apartment into new.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Як до́бре! А де вона́?
lines.source: That's great! And where is it?
lines.source_literal: How good! And where it?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Бі́ля вели́кого па́рку. Усі́ ві́кна вихо́дять на парк.
lines.source: Near a big park. All the windows look out onto the park.
lines.source_literal: Near big park. All windows go-out onto park.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А як ти перевезе́ш свої́ ре́чі? У те́бе ду́же бага́то книг.
lines.source: And how will you move your things? You have a lot of books.
lines.source_literal: And how you will-transport-across own things? At you very many of-books.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Та́то все перевезе́. Але́ споча́тку все тре́ба ви́нести з кварти́ри.
lines.source: Dad will take everything over. But first everything has to be carried out of the apartment.
lines.source_literal: Dad everything will-transport-across. But first everything necessary to-carry-out from apartment.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я допоможу́. О котрі́й прийти́?
lines.source: I'll help. What time should I come?
lines.source_literal: I will-help. At which to-arrive?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Прихо́дь до ме́не о дев’я́тій. Коли́ ми все ви́несемо, ми пої́демо в нову́ кварти́ру.
lines.source: Come over to my place at nine. When we've carried everything out, we'll drive to the new apartment.
lines.source_literal: Come to me at ninth. When we everything will-carry-out, we will-go to new apartment.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Дале́ко ї́хати?
lines.source: Is it a long drive?
lines.source_literal: Far to-go?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ні, два́дцять хвили́н. А там усе́ тре́ба бу́де занести́ в кварти́ру.
lines.source: No, twenty minutes. And there everything will have to be carried into the apartment.
lines.source_literal: No, twenty of-minutes. And there everything necessary will-be to-carry-in into apartment.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре. А Сем при́йде?
lines.source: All right. And will Sam come?
lines.source_literal: Good. And Sam will-arrive?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: У субо́ту він ї́де до Льво́ва, але́ обіця́в зайти́ в неді́лю на чай.
lines.source: On Saturday he's going to Lviv, but he promised to drop in for tea on Sunday.
lines.source_literal: In Saturday he goes to Lviv, but promised to-drop-in in Sunday for tea.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тоді́ до субо́ти! Я прийду́ о дев’я́тій.
lines.source: See you on Saturday, then! I'll be there at nine.
lines.source_literal: Then until Saturday! I will-arrive at ninth.

dialogues.title: An hour late
dialogues.context: Sam comes into Iryna Petrivna's class an hour late. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, до́брий день. Ми почали́ о во́сьмій. Чому́ ви прийшли́ о дев’я́тій?
lines.source: Hello, Sam. We started at eight. Why have you come at nine?
lines.source_literal: Sam, good day. We began at eighth. Why you arrived at ninth?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ви́бачте, Іри́но Петрі́вно. Я ви́йшов із до́му, як завжди́, о сьо́мій.
lines.source: I'm sorry, Iryna Petrivna. I left home at seven, as always.
lines.source_literal: Excuse, Iryna Petrivna. I went-out from home, as always, at seventh.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А по́тім?
lines.source: And then?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я прийшо́в на зупи́нку, але́ авто́бус до́вго не прихо́див.
lines.source: I got to the stop, but the bus didn't come for a long time.
lines.source_literal: I arrived to stop, but bus long not arrived.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А коли́ він прийшо́в?
lines.source: And when did it come?
lines.source_literal: And when it arrived?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Че́рез два́дцять хвили́н. А в авто́бусі я чита́в кни́гу й прої́хав свою́ зупи́нку.
lines.source: Twenty minutes later. And on the bus I was reading a book and rode past my stop.
lines.source_literal: Through twenty of-minutes. And in bus I read book and passed own stop.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: І що ви зроби́ли?
lines.source: And what did you do?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я ви́йшов на насту́пній зупи́нці й пів годи́ни йшов до університе́ту.
lines.source: I got off at the next stop and walked to the university for half an hour.
lines.source_literal: I went-out at next stop and half of-hour went to university.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Розумі́ю. Ви зазвича́й прихо́дите о во́сьмій. Захо́дьте, ми чита́ємо про Золоті́ воро́та.
lines.source: I understand. You usually come at eight. Come in, we're reading about the Golden Gate.
lines.source_literal: I-understand. You usually arrive at eighth. Come-in, we read about Golden Gates.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую. За́втра я ви́йду з до́му о шо́стій!
lines.source: Thank you. Tomorrow I'll leave home at six!
lines.source_literal: I-thank. Tomorrow I will-go-out from home at sixth!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: О шо́стій не тре́ба, Се́ме. Але́ в авто́бусі кра́ще не чита́йте.
lines.source: You don't need to leave at six, Sam. But you'd better not read on the bus.
lines.source_literal: At sixth not necessary, Sam. But in bus better not read.

grammar.title: Prefixes that give a movement its direction
grammar.explanation:
A prefix is a short part added to the front of a word that changes its meaning. Ukrainian adds prefixes to the verbs of motion to say how a movement relates to a place: whether it ends there, starts there, goes into it, across it, past it or around it. English says this with a separate word after the verb, as in 'come in', 'go out' and 'walk past'. Ukrainian puts it at the front of the verb: 'ви́йти', to go out, is 'ви-' added to 'йти'.

Each prefix keeps its meaning with every verb of motion. The ten common prefixes, shown with 'іти́', are:

- 'при-', arriving: 'прийти́', to arrive, to come
- 'ви-', going out: 'ви́йти', to go out, to leave
- 'у-' or 'в-', going in: 'увійти́', to enter
- 'за-', dropping in on the way, or going into: 'зайти́', to drop in
- 'пере-', crossing, or moving to a new place: 'перейти́', to cross
- 'від-', moving away: 'відійти́', to step away
- 'до-', reaching a goal: 'дійти́', to reach
- 'про-', passing through or past: 'пройти́', to pass
- 'під-', approaching: 'підійти́', to come up to
- 'об-', going around: 'обійти́', to go around

The same prefixes go on 'ї́хати' for a movement by vehicle:

- 'приї́хати', to arrive by vehicle
- 'ви́їхати', to drive out, to leave
- 'в’ї́хати', to drive in
- 'дої́хати', to reach by vehicle
- 'переї́хати', to cross by vehicle, and also to move house
- 'прої́хати', to pass by vehicle: 'прої́хати свою́ зупи́нку', to ride past one's stop

They go on the other verbs of motion too:

- 'принести́', to bring
- 'ви́нести', to carry out
- 'занести́', to carry in
- 'перевезти́', to move things by vehicle to a new place
- 'прилеті́ти', to arrive by plane

'Увійти́' and 'зайти́' both lead inside. 'Увійти́' names the entering itself and belongs more to careful speech and writing; after a vowel it is 'ввійти́', by the euphony rules. 'Зайти́' is the everyday word for going into a room, a shop or a café, and the usual word for a short visit on the way somewhere: 'зайти́ в апте́ку', to pop into the pharmacy.

Why 'іти́' is spelled 'йти' in 'прийти́' but 'ійти' in 'відійти́' is explained in the note on spelling and sound.

rows: Taras stepped away from the window.
We got as far as the park.
Olena went up to the window.
My parents have come to see us.

examples.source: When will you get home?
Excuse me, where is the exit?
I'll bring you a coffee.
The plane has arrived from Odesa.

grammar.title: Aspect: a perfective from one direction, an imperfective from the general verb
grammar.explanation:
A prefix does more than add a direction: it also decides the aspect. This is the main rule of the unit.

- A prefix on the verb of one direction makes a perfective verb: 'іти́' gives 'прийти́', and 'ї́хати' gives 'приї́хати'. It names one completed movement with its result: 'Сем прийшо́в.', Sam has come, and he is here.
- The same prefix on the general verb makes its imperfective partner: 'ходи́ти' gives 'прихо́дити'. It names the movement as a process, a repetition or a plain fact: 'Тара́с прихо́дить на робо́ту о дев’я́тій.', Taras gets to work at nine.

Once a prefix is added, the difference between movement in one direction and movement in general disappears. 'Прихо́дити' does not mean arriving in many directions or there and back; it is simply the imperfective partner of 'прийти́', and the two work like 'чита́ти' and 'прочита́ти'. The choice between them follows the rules of the unit on aspect:

- one completed arrival takes the perfective: 'Батьки́ приї́дуть за́втра.' (My parents will arrive tomorrow)
- a repeated arrival takes the imperfective: 'Сем приїжджа́є до Льво́ва ко́жного мі́сяця.' (Sam comes to Lviv every month)
- an arrival that kept not happening takes the imperfective: 'Авто́бус до́вго не прихо́див.' (The bus did not come for a long time)

For 'ї́хати' the imperfective is built on '-їжджа́ти', with the same 'ждж' as 'ї́жджу': 'приї́хати' and 'приїжджа́ти', 'ви́їхати' and 'виїжджа́ти', 'переї́хати' and 'переїжджа́ти'. These verbs in '-їжджа́ти' are regular first conjugation verbs, like 'чита́ти': 'приїжджа́ю', 'приїжджа́єш', 'приїжджа́ють'. The other verbs of motion pair in the same way: 'принести́' and 'прино́сити', to bring on foot; 'привезти́' and 'приво́зити', to bring by vehicle.

The perfectives built on 'йти' conjugate like 'іти́' and 'піти́'. Their present-looking forms are futures, as with every perfective: 'прийду́', I will come; 'при́йдеш', you will come. Their past ends like 'ішо́в': 'прийшо́в', 'прийшла́', 'прийшли́'. The imperfectives in '-хо́дити' conjugate like 'ходи́ти', with 'дж' in the 'я' form: 'прихо́джу', 'прихо́диш'.

The imperfective past of an arrival can also say that a visitor came and has left again: 'До те́бе прихо́див Тара́с.', Taras came to see you. The perfective 'Тара́с прийшо́в.' says that he is here now.

grammar.title: The preposition that goes with each prefix
grammar.explanation:
The prefix and the preposition after it often carry the same idea, and most prefixes have a regular partner:

- 'ви́йти з' and the genitive: out of a place ('ви́йти з до́му', 'з метро́')
- 'прийти́', 'зайти́', 'увійти́' with 'у', 'в' or 'на' and the accusative, or 'до' and the genitive: the place reached ('прийти́ на робо́ту', 'зайти́ до Андрі́я', 'увійти́ в кімна́ту')
- 'дійти́ до' and the genitive: as far as a goal ('дійти́ до па́рку')
- 'підійти́ до' and the genitive: up to something or someone ('підійти́ до вікна́')
- 'відійти́ від' and the genitive: away from ('відійти́ від вікна́')
- 'перейти́' and the accusative, with or without 'че́рез': across ('перейти́ ву́лицю', 'перейти́ че́рез ву́лицю')
- 'пройти́ повз' and the accusative: past ('пройти́ повз музе́й')
- 'пройти́ че́рез' and the accusative: through ('пройти́ че́рез парк')
- 'обійти́' and the accusative, with no preposition: around ('обійти́ парк')

Three prepositions are new.

'Від' takes the genitive and means away from. It stands beside 'з', out of: you come 'з до́му', out of the house, but step 'від вікна́', away from the window. For people 'від' is the only choice, the mirror of 'до': 'Я йду до бабу́сі.' (I'm going to Grandma's) and 'Я йду від бабу́сі.' (I'm coming from Grandma's).

'Повз' takes the accusative and means past, by: 'Ми прої́хали повз університе́т.' (We drove past the university.)

'Уздо́вж' takes the genitive and means along. By the euphony rules it is 'вздовж' after a vowel: 'Тара́с біг уздо́вж Дніпра́.', but 'Ми йшли вздовж Дніпра́.'

A place that takes 'на' for the goal takes 'з' for the starting point, as the A2 consolidation unit showed: 'прийти́ на по́шту', 'ви́йти з по́шти'.

'Додо́му' is an adverb meaning home, to one's home, built from 'до' and 'дім'. It answers 'куди́?' as 'вдо́ма' answers 'де?': 'Я йду додо́му.' (I'm going home) against 'Я вдо́ма.' (I'm at home). From home is two words, 'з до́му'.

grammar.title: Giving directions and inviting: imperatives and questions
grammar.explanation:
Directions and descriptions of a route use three forms of the prefixed verbs:

- the perfective imperative for each step, because each step is one completed movement, as in a recipe: 'Ви́йдіть із метро́ й перейді́ть пло́щу.' (Come out of the metro and cross the square)
- the perfective future for a route told as what will happen: 'Ви ви́йдете з метро́ й пере́йдете пло́щу.' (You'll come out of the metro and cross the square)
- the imperfective present for the route someone takes every time: 'Я вихо́джу з метро́ й перехо́джу пло́щу.' (I come out of the metro and cross the square)

The imperatives of the perfectives in 'йти' are built like 'іди́', 'іді́ть', with the stress on the ending: 'прийди́', 'прийді́ть'; 'зайди́', 'зайді́ть'; 'перейди́', 'перейді́ть'; 'пройди́', 'пройді́ть'; 'дійди́', 'дійді́ть'; 'відійди́', 'відійді́ть'. The verbs with 'ви-' keep the stress on 'ви-' in every form but take the same endings: 'ви́йди', 'ви́йдіть'. The rule from the unit on the imperative looks at the stress of the 'я' form, and in 'ви́йду' that stress sits on the prefix, not on the verb, so the ending is the one 'іду́' has: '-и', '-іть'.

'Ї́хати' follows the rule: 'ї́ду' is stressed on the stem, so its imperative has no ending, 'їдь', 'ї́дьте', and its perfectives keep it: 'приї́дь', 'приї́дьте'.

An invitation takes the imperfective, as the unit on the imperative showed. The imperfectives in '-хо́дити' are stressed on the stem in the 'я' form, so their imperatives have no ending, and those in '-їжджа́ти' have a stem that ends in a vowel, so they take '-й':

- 'Прихо́дь!', 'Прихо́дьте!': Come over!
- 'Захо́дь!', 'Захо́дьте!': Come in!
- 'Приїжджа́й!', 'Приїжджа́йте!': Come and visit!, to someone in another place

A negative imperative is imperfective too: 'Не перехо́дьте ву́лицю тут.' (Don't cross the street here.)

A question made of an infinitive, alone or after a question word, with no other verb, asks what to do, like English 'shall I' or 'how do I': 'Як дійти́ до па́рку?' (How do I get to the park on foot?), 'Як дої́хати до це́нтру?' (How do I get downtown by bus or car?), 'Зайти́ туди́?' (Shall I drop in there?). The person who is to act can be added in the dative: 'Куди́ мені́ йти?' (Where should I go?, literally 'where-to to-me to-go?').

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: прийти́, відійти́, від’ї́хати, приїжджа́ти and ви́хід
grammar.explanation:
Every new word of this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The prefixes bring up the points below.

'Іти́' has two spellings, 'іти́' and 'йти', and the euphony rules write 'йти' after a vowel. A prefix that ends in a vowel is therefore followed by 'йти':

- 'при-' and 'йти': 'прийти́' [prɪjˈtɪ]
- 'ви-' and 'йти': 'ви́йти' [ˈʋɪjtɪ]
- 'за-' and 'йти': 'зайти́'
- 'пере-' and 'йти': 'перейти́'
- 'про-' and 'йти': 'пройти́'

In all of them 'й' is a consonant, so 'прийти́' has two syllables, as its two vowel letters show.

A prefix that ends in a consonant takes an 'і' before 'йти', so that three consonants do not meet: 'від-', 'під-' and 'об-' give 'відійти́', 'підійти́' and 'обійти́', and 'в-' gives 'увійти́'. 'До-' becomes 'ді-' before 'йти': 'дійти́', the way 'по-' with 'йти' became 'піти́'. Where no 'йти' follows it stays 'до-': 'дохо́дити', 'дої́хати'. The past keeps the spelling of the infinitive: 'прийшо́в', 'відійшо́в', 'дійшо́в'.

The unit on soft sounds taught the apostrophe after 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' and 'р' before 'я', 'ю', 'є' and 'ї'. Where a prefix ends in a consonant, the apostrophe is written before these letters after any consonant, 'д' included: 'в’ї́хати', 'від’ї́хати' [ʋʲidˈjixɑtɪ], 'під’ї́хати', 'об’ї́хати'. It shows that the consonant stays hard and that the [j] of 'ї' is said in full. After a prefix that ends in a vowel no apostrophe is needed, because 'ї' always adds its [j]: 'приї́хати' [prɪˈjixɑtɪ], 'заї́хати', 'переї́хати'.

The imperfectives in '-їжджа́ти' have the 'ждж' of 'ї́жджу', said [ʒd͡ʒ] with no vowel between the two sounds: 'приїжджа́ти' [prɪjiʒˈd͡ʒɑtɪ]. Their stress stays on the 'а' after 'ждж' in every form: 'приїжджа́ю', 'приїжджа́єш'.

The imperfectives in '-хо́дити' are stressed on 'хо' in every form: 'прихо́дити', 'прихо́джу', 'прихо́диш', unlike 'ходи́ти' and 'ходжу́'.

Apart from those with 'ви-', the perfectives in 'йти' move their stress. The 'я' form is stressed on the ending, and the other future forms on the vowel before 'йд': 'прийду́', 'при́йдеш', 'при́йдуть'; 'зайду́', 'за́йдеш'; 'перейду́', 'пере́йдеш'; 'відійду́', 'віді́йдеш'. The past and the imperative keep the stress on the ending: 'прийшо́в', 'прийди́'.

'Ви-' takes the stress in every form of a perfective verb, as in 'ви́грати': 'ви́йти', 'ви́йду', 'ви́йдеш', 'ви́йшов', 'ви́йдіть', 'ви́їхати', 'ви́нести'. The imperfective partner is not stressed on it: 'вихо́дити', 'виїжджа́ти'.

'Ви́хід' and 'вхід' are nouns built on the stem of 'ходи́ти'. The 'о' becomes 'і' in the closed last syllable and comes back where the syllable opens, the alternation of 'кіт', 'кота́': 'ви́хід', 'ви́ходу'; 'вхід', 'вхо́ду'. 'Ха́рків', 'Ха́ркова' and 'воро́та', 'ворі́т' in the readings show the same alternation, like 'Львів', 'Льво́ва'.

The other new words:

- 'Повз' has 'в' before a consonant, said [w], and keeps its voiced 'з' at the end: [pɔwz].
- 'Від' keeps its voiced [d] at the end.
- 'Уздо́вж' ends in 'вж', said [wʒ]: [uzˈdɔwʒ].
- 'Воро́та', gate, in the third dialogue and the first reading, is a plural-only noun: one gate is 'воро́та', with plural adjectives and verbs ('Золоті́ воро́та стоя́ть'). Its genitive 'ворі́т' has no ending, so its 'о' becomes 'і'.
- 'Золоті́' in 'Золоті́ воро́та', the Golden Gate, is the plural of 'золоти́й', golden.
- 'Доро́га', road, way, in the readings, is the noun inside 'Щасли́вої доро́ги!'.
- 'Невели́кий', small, in the first reading, is 'не' and 'вели́кий'.
- 'Ва́жко', hard, in the second reading, is a predicative word from 'важки́й', as 'ле́гко' is from 'легки́й'.
- 'Ре́чі', things, in the second dialogue, is the plural of 'річ', thing, the word inside 'до ре́чі'; 'е' becomes 'і' in the closed syllable of 'річ'.
- 'Марко́', a man's name, has the vocative 'Ма́рку', with the stress moved to the first syllable.
- 'Дзвіни́ця', bell tower, in the first reading, comes from 'дзвін', bell, the word behind 'дзво́ник' and 'дзвони́ти'; 'дз' is one sound, [d͡z].

culture.title: A new home: the cat goes in first
culture.text:
A move to a new home is a big event in Ukraine, and many families keep old customs for it. The best known is the cat. Before anyone else, the family lets a cat into the new home: 'Пе́ршим у нову́ ха́ту захо́дить кіт.' (The cat goes into the new house first.) People say that a cat finds the best and calmest place in a home, and that the first one to cross the threshold takes on any bad luck the house holds. Some families also carry bread and salt into the new home first, an old symbol of welcome and a wish that the household will never go hungry.

A few weeks after the move, the family invites friends and relatives to 'новосі́лля', the housewarming party. The word is built from 'нови́й', new, and the root of 'осели́тися', to settle, so it says 'a new settling'; its doubled 'лл' is one long soft [lʲː]. Guests bring practical gifts for the home and greet the hosts with 'З новосі́ллям!', literally 'with housewarming!', in the same way as 'З днем наро́дження!' on a birthday.

Moving within a city is common, because many young people rent their apartments. The phrases heard most often around a move are:

- 'переї́хати в нову́ кварти́ру': to move into a new apartment
- 'переї́хати до і́ншого мі́ста': to move to another city
- 'Приїжджа́й у го́сті!': Come and visit!, literally 'arrive into guests'

readings.title: A walk from the Golden Gate to Saint Sophia's Cathedral

paragraphs.target: Від Золоти́х ворі́т до Софі́йського собо́ру мо́жна дійти́ за де́сять хвили́н. Доро́га коро́тка, але́ ду́же ціка́ва. Почні́ть бі́ля метро́. Коли́ ви ви́йдете з метро́, Золоті́ воро́та бу́дуть пе́ред ва́ми.
paragraphs.source: From the Golden Gate you can walk to Saint Sophia's Cathedral in ten minutes. The way is short but very interesting. Start by the metro. When you come out of the metro, the Golden Gate will be in front of you.
paragraphs.source_literal: From Golden Gates to Sophia's cathedral possible to-reach within ten of-minutes. Way short, but very interesting. Begin near metro. When you will-go-out from metro, Golden Gates will-be before you.

paragraphs.target: В одина́дцятому столі́тті тут був вхід до Ки́єва. Че́рез ці воро́та лю́ди вхо́дили в мі́сто й виїжджа́ли з ньо́го. Сього́дні тут стоя́ть нові́ воро́та, а в них невели́кий музе́й.
paragraphs.source: In the eleventh century this was the entrance to Kyiv. People walked into the city and rode out of it through this gate. Today a new gate stands here, with a small museum inside.
paragraphs.source_literal: In eleventh century here was entrance to Kyiv. Through these gates people went-in into city and drove-out from it. Today here stand new gates, and in them small museum.

paragraphs.target: Відійді́ть від ворі́т і йдіть уздо́вж Володи́мирської ву́лиці. Ви про́йдете повз кафе́ й магази́ни, а за кі́лька хвили́н ді́йдете до вели́кої пло́щі. Це Софі́йська пло́ща.
paragraphs.source: Step away from the gate and walk along Volodymyrska Street. You will pass cafés and shops, and in a few minutes you will reach a big square. This is Saint Sophia's Square.
paragraphs.source_literal: Step-away from gates and go along Volodymyr's street. You will-pass past cafés and shops, and within several of-minutes will-reach to big square. This Sophia's square.

paragraphs.target: Перейді́ть пло́щу. Пе́ред ва́ми бу́де висо́ка дзвіни́ця. Пройді́ть під не́ю, і ви ді́йдете до собо́ру. Софі́йський собо́р стої́ть тут з одина́дцятого столі́ття.
paragraphs.source: Cross the square. In front of you there will be a tall bell tower. Walk through under it, and you will reach the cathedral. Saint Sophia's Cathedral has stood here since the eleventh century.
paragraphs.source_literal: Cross square. Before you will-be tall bell-tower. Pass under it, and you will-reach to cathedral. Sophia's cathedral stands here from eleventh century.

paragraphs.target: Якщо́ у вас ще є час, ви́йдіть на пло́щу й перейді́ть її́ ще раз. За п’ять хвили́н ви ді́йдете до Миха́йлівського собо́ру. Він си́ній, тому́ його́ ле́гко знайти́.
paragraphs.source: If you still have time, go back out onto the square and cross it once more. In five minutes you will reach Saint Michael's Cathedral. It is blue, so it is easy to find.

questions.explanation: 'Обійти́' with the accusative is to go around something, and 'обійти́ все мі́сто' is to walk all over the city.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian verbs with their meanings

exercises.audio_target: Я ви́йшов із до́му о сьо́мій.

exercises.prompt: Which prefix says that a movement goes out of a place?
exercises.explanation: 'Ви-' means out: 'ви́йти', to go out. 'При-' is arriving, 'за-' dropping in and 'під-' approaching.

exercises.audio_target: Ми перейшли́ пло́щу й пішли́ ліво́руч.
choices: We walked around the square and went left.
We crossed the square and went right.
We crossed the square and went left.

exercises.prompt_target: Сем ___ із метро́ й пішо́в до па́рку.
exercises.hint_source: Sam came out of the metro and walked to the park.
exercises.explanation: Out of a place is 'ви-' with 'з' or 'із' and the genitive. The past of 'ви́йти' is 'ви́йшов', stressed on 'ви-'.
'За-' is the prefix of a short visit on the way somewhere. Walking past is 'пройти́ повз апте́ку', and leaving is 'ви́йти з апте́ки'.

exercises.hint_source: We walked past the museum and the bank.
exercises.explanation: 'Повз' means past and takes the accusative; for these inanimate nouns it looks like the nominative.

exercises.prompt: Match the phrases with their meanings

exercises.audio_target: Бабу́ся приїжджа́є до нас ко́жного лі́та.
choices: Grandma comes to see us every summer.
Grandma came to see us last summer.
Grandma comes to see us every winter.

exercises.hint_source: Sam is coming from Iryna Petrivna's.
exercises.explanation: Coming from a person is 'від' and the genitive, the mirror of 'до' for going to a person. 'З' means out of a place.

exercises.prompt: Sam arrives at eight every day. Which form completes 'Сем щодня́ ___ о во́сьмій.'?
exercises.explanation: A repeated arrival takes the imperfective 'прихо́дити', here in the present. 'При́йде' is the perfective future, one arrival, and 'прийшо́в' is one completed arrival in the past.

exercises.hint_source: Do you often come to Kyiv?
exercises.explanation: Coming from another city is a movement by vehicle, and 'ча́сто' asks for the imperfective: 'приїжджа́ти', 'приїжджа́єш'.

exercises.prompt: Which verb is the imperfective partner of 'приї́хати'?
exercises.explanation: For 'ї́хати' the prefixed imperfective is built on '-їжджа́ти'. 'Пої́хати' is a perfective meaning to set off, and 'ї́здити' is the unprefixed general verb.

exercises.prompt_target: Тара́с ти́ждень не ___ на робо́ту, бо хворі́в.
exercises.hint_source: Taras didn't come to work for a week because he was ill.
exercises.explanation: Arrivals that did not happen over a period take the imperfective: 'не прихо́див' for a whole week.

exercises.prompt: 'До те́бе прихо́див Тара́с.' What does this sentence tell you?
choices: Taras came to see you and has left again.
Taras is on his way to you now.
Taras will come to see you tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: The imperfective past of an arrival can say that the visitor came and went away again. 'Тара́с прийшо́в' would say that he is here now.

exercises.prompt_target: Мій брат ___ до Оде́си мину́лого ро́ку.
exercises.hint_source: My brother moved to Odesa last year.
exercises.explanation: Moving house is 'переї́хати', one completed move, so the perfective past: 'переї́хав' for a man.

exercises.hint_source: Excuse me, how do I get to the university?
exercises.explanation: A question word with an infinitive asks how to do something. 'Дійти́' asks the way on foot and 'дої́хати' by bus or car; both take 'до' and the genitive. 'Пройти́' and 'прої́хати' ask which way to go.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the imperative of 'ви́йти' for 'ви'?
exercises.explanation: 'Ви́йдіть' takes the ending of 'іді́ть' and keeps the stress on 'ви-'. 'Ви́йдете' is the future, you will go out, and 'ви́йшли' the past.

exercises.prompt_target: Перейді́ть пло́щу, а по́тім ___ уздо́вж ву́лиці.
exercises.hint_source: Cross the square, and then walk along the street.
exercises.explanation: Each step of directions to someone you call 'ви' is an imperative: 'іді́ть', or 'пройді́ть' for walking a stretch of the street. After the consonant of 'по́тім' the euphony rules write 'іді́ть'.

exercises.prompt_target: ___, будь ла́ска, ка́ва вже на столі́!
exercises.hint_source: Come in, please, the coffee is already on the table!
exercises.explanation: An invitation takes the imperfective imperative: 'захо́дьте' to 'ви', 'захо́дь' to 'ти'; 'прохо́дьте' and 'прохо́дь' also invite a guest in. The 'я' form 'захо́джу' is stressed on the stem, so there is no ending.

choices: After a prefix that ends in a consonant, an 'і' comes before 'йти'.
The stress mark needs an extra vowel after 'від-'.
exercises.explanation: 'При-' ends in a vowel and is followed by 'йти'. 'Від-' ends in a consonant, and the 'і' keeps three consonants from meeting: 'відійти́', 'підійти́', 'обійти́'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'від’ї́хати' have an apostrophe but 'приї́хати' does not?
choices: The apostrophe marks the stressed syllable.
The apostrophe is written only after 'д'.
After a prefix that ends in a consonant, the apostrophe keeps the consonant hard and the [j] of 'ї' said in full.
exercises.explanation: At the end of a prefix the apostrophe goes after any consonant before 'я', 'ю', 'є' and 'ї': 'в’ї́хати', 'від’ї́хати', 'об’ї́хати'. After a vowel, 'ї' adds its [j] by itself.

exercises.prompt: Where is the stress in the forms of the perfective verb 'ви́йти'?
choices: On the ending, in every form
On the prefix 'ви-', in every form
On the prefix in the infinitive only
exercises.explanation: A perfective verb with 'ви-' is stressed on the prefix in every form: 'ви́йду', 'ви́йшов', 'ви́йдіть'. Its imperfective partner 'вихо́дити' is not.

choices: Olena stepped away from the window.
Olena went up to the window.
Olena went up to the bus.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'ви́хід' written with 'і' but its genitive 'ви́ходу' with 'о'?
choices: 'О' becomes 'і' in a closed last syllable and comes back when the syllable opens, as in 'кіт', 'кота́'.
exercises.explanation: In 'ви́хід' the last syllable ends in a consonant, so the 'о' of 'ходи́ти' becomes 'і'. The ending '-у' opens the syllable again: 'ви́ходу'.

exercises.hint_source: We'll get off at the next stop.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why does Sam tell Marko not to take a taxi?
choices: Taxis are expensive at the station.
Sam lives close to the station.
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'Не бери́ таксі́, я живу́ бли́зько.'

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, what will Taras do on Saturday?
choices: Drive Oksana's things to the new apartment
Come at nine and help carry everything out
exercises.explanation: Oksana says 'Прихо́дь до ме́не о дев’я́тій', and Taras answers 'Я прийду́ о дев’я́тій.' Her father moves the things, and Sam goes to Lviv.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, why did Sam arrive at nine?
choices: The bus came late, and then he rode past his stop.
He dropped in at a café on the way.
exercises.explanation: 'Авто́бус до́вго не прихо́див', and then 'я чита́в кни́гу й прої́хав свою́ зупи́нку'. He left home at seven, as always.

exercises.hint_source: We came out onto the square.

exercises.prompt_source: Cross the street at the traffic light.
They were walking along the street.
After work I'll drop in on Andrii.
Oksana left the apartment at eight.
answers: Окса́на ви́йшла з кварти́ри о во́сьмій.
О во́сьмій Окса́на ви́йшла з кварти́ри.
exercises.explanation: One completed departure takes the perfective 'ви́йти', here 'ви́йшла' for a woman, and the place left takes 'з' and the genitive: 'з кварти́ри'.

exercises.prompt_source: Come over to our place on Saturday! (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: An invitation takes the imperfective imperative, here 'прихо́дь' for 'ти', or 'приїжджа́й' for a friend who will come by vehicle. The people visited take 'до' and the genitive, 'до нас'.

exercises.prompt_source: Olena will come home at six.
exercises.explanation: One future arrival takes the perfective future: 'при́йде' on foot, or 'приї́де' by vehicle. 'Додо́му' says home as a direction.
'Перейти́' takes the street in the accusative, with or without 'че́рез'.
